lesson.title: From Critical Points to Best Possible Outcomes
lesson.summary: Optimization uses critical numbers together with the Candidates Test to find the true largest or smallest value a function can take on an interval, not merely its local ups and downs, which is what makes calculus useful for real decisions.
lesson.body:
Everything covered so far, critical numbers, the First and Second Derivative Tests, concavity, inflection points, describes local behavior: what happens near one particular point on a graph. Optimization asks a bigger question. Out of every value a function can take, which one is truly the largest, and which is truly the smallest? These are called the absolute, or global, maximum and minimum, and they are not the same thing as a local maximum or minimum. A function can have several local peaks without any of them being the single highest point overall.

The tool for finding a global extremum on a closed interval [a, b] is the Candidates Test, sometimes called the closed interval method. If f is continuous on [a, b], the Extreme Value Theorem guarantees that f actually attains an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum somewhere on that interval. Any absolute extremum that occurs at an interior point must also be a local extremum, which means it must occur at a critical number. The only other place an absolute extremum can occur is at one of the two endpoints, since the interior reasoning does not apply there. So the full list of candidates is short: every critical number inside (a, b), plus the two endpoints a and b. Evaluate f at each candidate. The largest value is the absolute maximum, and the smallest is the absolute minimum.

Apply this to the running example, f(x) = 2x^3 - 3x^2 - 12x + 5, restricted to the closed interval [-2, 3]. Local extrema analysis already found the critical numbers x = -1 and x = 2, and both lie inside this interval. The candidates are therefore x = -2, -1, 2, and 3. Evaluating: f(-2) = 2(-8) - 3(4) + 24 + 5 = -16 - 12 + 24 + 5 = 1. f(-1) = 12, computed earlier. f(2) = -15, also computed earlier. f(3) = 2(27) - 3(9) - 36 + 5 = 54 - 27 - 36 + 5 = -4. Comparing all four values, 1, 12, -15, and -4, the absolute maximum is 12 at x = -1, and the absolute minimum is -15 at x = 2.

In this particular case the interior local extrema turned out to also be the global extrema, since neither endpoint value came close to matching them. That is not guaranteed in general. Sometimes an endpoint outranks every interior critical number, which is exactly why the Candidates Test insists on checking every candidate, endpoints included, rather than assuming the local extremum you already found must be the biggest or smallest value overall.

This global extremum hunt is precisely what applied optimization problems are doing under the hood. Maximizing the area you can enclose, minimizing the distance from a point to a curve, minimizing the cost of a project, each one asks for a true global best, not just a local peak or dip. The difference in the chapters ahead is that the function to analyze will not arrive ready made in algebra. It has to be built first from a written description of a real situation, which is exactly the skill the next few chapters develop.
